extracted.intended_audience: parents and tutors (especially of boys of quality); educators and those choosing pedagogy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on selecting tutors and methods for educating children (especially aristocratic boys), emphasizing judgment, manners, experiential learning, and tailoring instruction to the pupil's nature rather than rote accumulation of letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of personal wisdom over borrowed learning
rubrics_metrics.description: A man can never be wise but by his own wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne rejects 'relative and mendicant understanding' (learning only from others). True wisdom must come from one's own judgment and internalized understanding rather than mere accumulation of others' learning or citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer judgement over mere knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is not so absolutely necessary as judgment; the last may make shift without the other, but the other never without this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a pupil or candidate (e.g., for office), place greater weight on capacity for judgement and understanding than on mere possession of facts or letters. Examples: some parliaments test only learning, others also test understanding — the latter is superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning must be assimilated and alter the person
rubrics_metrics.description: We are not to tie learning to the soul, but to work and incorporate them together: not to tincture it only, but to give it a thorough and perfect dye; which, if it will not take colour, and meliorate its imperfect state, it were without question better to let it alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should produce inward change and practical habits, not superficial adornment. If study does not 'meliorate' and change the pupil's character, it is of little value; unassimilated learning can be worse than none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tutors who produce vanity (pedants) rather than practical sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedants appear to be deprived even of common sense; their Latin and Greek have only made them a greater coxcomb...they have the theory of all things, let who will put it in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware instructors who teach parade-knowledge that swells the pupil with 'vain and empty shreds,' producing arrogance without sound judgement or practical ability. Prefer teachers who cultivate sense and judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a tutor who forms a 'well-made head' over a 'well-filled' one
rubrics_metrics.description: For a boy of quality ... I would, also, have his friends solicitous to find him out a tutor, who has rather a well-made than a well-filled head ... seeking, indeed, both the one and the other, but rather of the two to prefer manners and judgment to mere learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting a tutor, prioritize capacity for shaping character, manners, and judgement (a 'tete bien faite') rather than merely filling the pupil with facts or citations. The tutor should exercise discretion in method and favor formation of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active, Socratic method: have pupils speak and test themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates, and since him Arcesilaus, made first their scholars speak, and then they spoke to them ... he should also hear his pupil speak in turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should encourage pupils to express themselves, test their own understanding, and learn by spoken engagement. The authority of the teacher should not shut down the learner's active participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess learning by application, not memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the master not only examine him about the grammatical construction of the bare words of his lesson, but about the sense and let him judge of the profit he has made, not by the testimony of his memory, but by that of his life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should measure whether the pupil can apply and adapt knowledge in life and practice rather than merely repeat memorized text. The 'profit' of study is seen in behavior and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require transfer: make pupils put learning into many forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him make him put what he has learned into a hundred several forms, and accommodate it to so many several subjects, to see if he yet rightly comprehends it, and has made it his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage exercises that force adaptation and rephrasing of learned material across contexts to confirm genuine understanding and ownership of ideas (Plato's pedagogic institutions referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate instruction to pupil's capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Such as, according to our common way of teaching, undertake, with one and the same lesson, and the same measure of direction, to instruct several boys of differing and unequal capacities, are infinitely mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-size-fits-all teaching. Teachers must adjust pace, content, and method to each pupil's natural ability; otherwise most pupils will gain little. 'Put him, like a young horse, trot before him, that he may judge of his going.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach by works and examples, not only by words and hearsay
rubrics_metrics.description: They thought fit, at first hand, to initiate their children with the knowledge of effects, and to instruct them, not by hearsay and rote, but by the experiment of action, in lively forming and moulding them; not only by words and precepts, but chiefly by works and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experiential education (practice, examples, roles/tests) — as in Spartan and Persian models — so knowledge becomes habit and capability rather than mere theoretical learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should cultivate virtue suited to the pupil's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s principal institution ... is to fit his citizens with employments suitable to their nature ... the eldest son ... instructed in religion ... to conquer his appetites and desires ... to despise all danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education must aim to form the moral and civic qualities required by the student's future station (e.g., courage, prudence, justice for leaders), rather than training for irrelevant academic display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overload learning when it will be corrupted by a bad disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is an excellent drug, but no drug has virtue enough to preserve itself from corruption and decay, if the vessel be tainted and impure wherein it is put to keep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching cannot cure a corrupted or unteachable soul; learning given to those who won't apply it or whose nature is 'vulgar' will be misused or wasted. Be realistic about the pupil's nature when choosing what and how to teach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary that certain kinds of study can soften martial vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples have demonstrated to us that in military affairs, and all others of the like active nature, the study of sciences more softens and untempers the courages of men than it in any way fortifies and excites them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the desired end is military or vigorous public service, excessive bookish study may be counterproductive; balance letters with physical and civic training appropriate to the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teachers who rely on authority to silence student inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Obest plerumque iis, qui discere volunt, auctoritas eorum, qui docent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher authority often impedes genuine learning; instructors should not use their status to prevent pupils from speaking, testing, and developing independent judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer teachers who evaluate progress by life and action rather than by school tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him judge of the profit he has made, not by the testimony of his memory, but by that of his life ... We do not study for life, but only for the school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction and assessment so that improvement is visible in conduct and practical competence, not merely in academic exercises. Avoid educating solely for school success disconnected from real life.
